hook: Your data lives in SQL Server today — and Postgres tomorrow. Python speaks both, and one skill transfers.

scenes.title: SQLAlchemy = **EF Core**, twice
scenes.sub: Core (SQL builder) and ORM (object mapper) under one roof
scenes.narration: SQLAlchemy is the standard Python database toolkit, and it mirrors EF Core so closely that you'll be productive in an hour. Two layers. Core: a SQL expression builder — Python code that compiles to SQL, explicit about queries, perfect for reports and analytics-shaped work. ORM: maps classes to tables — your objects save and load, relationships navigate, unit-of-work via session. Your C sharp instincts transfer directly: Core is like Dapper-plus, the ORM is like EF. Most real projects mix both.

items.s: One engine per database; the URL names the driver
Declarative classes; session.add/commit — the EF shape
Composable, parameterized SQL as Python objects

scenes.narration: The mental mapping. Engine — your connection string and configuration, created once. ORM layer: a Base class, columns as typed attributes, and a session that tracks changes — add, commit, exactly like DbContext. Core layer: table objects with a c attribute for columns, select-where-order expressions that compile to parameterized SQL. Both layers share the engine, transactions, and pooling. Rule of thumb: ORM for domain writes, Core (or plain text SQL) for analytics reads — same split you already make in C sharp.

scenes.title: pyodbc: the **bridge home**
scenes.sub: Your existing SQL Server estates, from Python
scenes.narration: At Deloitte, SQL Server is the gravity well — good news: the path is paved. pyodbc is the ODBC bridge: any database with an ODBC driver, including every SQL Server since forever. In practice you rarely touch pyodbc directly; SQLAlchemy's mssql-plus-pyodbc dialect sits on top, so the same ORM and Core code runs against MSSQL. Native client drivers, Windows auth, encrypted connections — all supported. Your first agent that reads the enterprise warehouse needs exactly this: one connection string, and fifteen years of schema is queryable from Python.

items.s: The connection URL; driver 18+ for modern encryption defaults
Windows and Entra-ID auth flow through ODBC — enterprise auth patterns intact
Core/ORM parameterize automatically; raw text SQL needs bound params

scenes.narration: Connection-string anatomy: dialect plus driver in the URL, modern ODBC Driver 18 for current encryption behavior, and enterprise authentication — trusted connection or Entra ID — flows through the same ODBC layer. One security note travels with you: the moment you write raw SQL text, the parameter-binding rules from Reel 7 are law — the ORM protects you; hand-written SQL must use bound parameters. This is the same SQL-Injection battle you've fought since ASP dot net, on a new front.

scenes.title: Connections are **expensive**. Reuse them.
scenes.sub: Pool sizing: the art of enough-but-not-too-many
scenes.narration: A database connection costs a handshake, memory server-side, and a seat in the license headcount. SQLAlchemy's engine pools by default: connections are checked out, used, and returned — your code never manages them explicitly. Sizing matters: too few and requests queue; too many and the database drowns. Start small — five to ten — and tune by watching wait times. And one async note: pooling works the same in async engines; each awaits its checkout. This is ADO dot net connection pooling wearing a Python jacket — same physics, same tuning instincts.

items.s: Create once at startup; sessions borrow and return
Baseline for services; scale out replicas before growing pools
Cheap liveness check — kills 'connection reset by peer' surprises

scenes.narration: Operational rules. One engine per database, created at application startup, injected everywhere — never per request. Pool size five with overflow ten is a sane service baseline; when saturated, prefer more app replicas over bigger pools — databases prefer many small polite clients to one giant rude one. And enable pre-ping: a lightweight liveness check on checkout that converts stale-connection errors into seamless reconnects. Five percent overhead, ninety-five percent fewer 2am pages.

scenes.title: Schema changes = **versioned migrations**
scenes.narration: Schema evolution without versioning is how databases become archaeology sites. Alembic is SQLAlchemy's migration tool — autogenerate compares your models to the live schema and drafts a migration script; you review, edit, commit. Upgrade and downgrade functions make changes reversible — the schema equivalent of rollback. Wire migrations into deployment: containers run alembic upgrade head at startup or as a release step. Your EF Migrations muscle memory maps one-to-one: snapshot the model, generate, review, apply, version.

items.s: Diff models vs database → a draft upgrade()/downgrade() script
Autogenerate drafts; destructive changes (drops) always hand-checked
Migrations run as a release step — schema and code ship together

scenes.narration: The workflow. Autogenerate to draft, eyeball the diff — especially drops and type changes, which autogenerate handles cautiously at best. Commit the migration with the code that needs it. Apply at release time: one command, versioned, logged. Downgrade functions matter more than they look — they're your drill for the day a deploy goes sideways at 3am. If your team has ever repaired a production schema by hand over a screenshare, Alembic is the vaccine — the exact same discipline as EF Migrations, which you already trust.

scenes.title: Postgres: the AI era's **default database**
scenes.sub: Free, everywhere, and extensible into vector land
scenes.narration: Why does every AI tutorial use Postgres? Three reasons. It's free and runs everywhere — Docker one-liner to managed cloud. Its ecosystem is the deepest in the open-source world — extensions for vectors, full-text search, JSON, time series, geospatial. And it scales honestly: from your laptop prototype to serious production without a rewrite. For your architecture work, the practical takeaway: prototype AI apps against Postgres locally in Docker, and the same SQL and drivers carry to any managed Postgres a client prefers. One skill, every environment.

items.s: Local dev parity in one container; pgAdmin or psql to explore
pgvector, pg_trgm, PostGIS, TimescaleDB — CREATE EXTENSION and go

scenes.narration: The onboarding path. Run Postgres 16 in Docker; connect with psql or a GUI; your SQLAlchemy code works unchanged — only the connection URL changes from mssql to postgresql. Then explore extensions, because they're why Postgres won AI: add pgvector and your relational database gains semantic search — which is the next chapter. Architect's take: in client conversations, 'Postgres plus extensions' is frequently the answer that satisfies security review, budget review, and the roadmap simultaneously. It's the new default, and it lives on your laptop today.

scenes.title: Vectors **inside** Postgres — pgvector
scenes.sub: One database for rows AND embeddings
scenes.narration: pgvector is the extension that turns Postgres into a vector database. Add a column of type vector with your dimension, insert embeddings alongside your rows, create an index — and SQL gains nearest-neighbor operators: order by embedding distance and limit k. The architectural elegance: your documents, metadata, permissions, and embeddings live in ONE store — joins between semantic search and relational filters are ordinary SQL. No sync pipelines, no second system to secure and back up. It won't out-scale dedicated vector databases — GA-10 covers that decision — but for a huge fraction of real workloads, one Postgres is the whole answer.

items.t: ALTER TABLE docs ADD COLUMN embedding vector(1536)
SELECT * FROM docs ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT 5
items.s: <=> = cosine distance · combine with WHERE tenant_id = $2 freely
Semantic search + filters + permissions in ONE system of record

scenes.narration: The essentials. Vector type sized to your model; an HNSW index for approximate nearest-neighbor speed — GA-09 explains the algorithm. The distance operator: less-equal-greater-than is cosine distance — order ascending, limit k. And the killer feature: filter freely — where tenant equals this, where date after that — vector and relational in one query, one transaction, one backup. For multi-tenant systems with moderate scale, this pattern deletes entire categories of integration risk. GA-10 puts pgvector on the selection matrix against the dedicated stores — with honest limits.

scenes.title: Databases wired. Now: search at scale
scenes.next: Reel 25 · Vector DB Fundamentals — ANN, recall, metadata filters, hybrid

recap: SQLAlchemy = Core (SQL builder) + ORM (EF twin); pyodbc/MSSQL and Postgres share both
One pooled engine app-wide (pre_ping=True); Alembic = EF Migrations for schema
Postgres + pgvector: rows, filters, permissions, and embeddings in one database

quiz.q: Which SQLAlchemy layer is the closest match to writing explicit, composable SQL?
quiz.why: Core is the SQL expression builder — parameterized, composable Python that compiles to SQL; the ORM is the object-mapping layer.

opts: Stale/dead connections being handed out from the pool (transparent reconnection)
quiz.why: A cheap liveness check on checkout turns 'connection reset by peer' errors into seamless reconnects — classic 2am-page eliminator.

quiz.q: What's the architectural appeal of pgvector for a multi-tenant RAG app?
opts: Embeddings, metadata filters, and tenant isolation live in ONE database — no sync pipeline or second system
quiz.why: Vector similarity and relational constraints (tenant_id, ACLs) in one query, one transaction, one backup — integration risk deleted.

code.title: SQLAlchemy + Postgres/pgvector in one script
code.body:
from sqlalchemy import create_engine, text

# Same code against SQL Server — only the URL changes:
# engine = create_engine("mssql+pyodbc://user:pw@server/db?driver=ODBC+Driver+18+for+SQL+Server")
engine = create_engine(
    "postgresql+psycopg://postgres:pw@localhost:5432/app",
    pool_size=5, max_overflow=10, pool_pre_ping=True,
)

# pgvector setup (once)
with engine.begin() as conn:
    conn.execute(text("CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS vector"))
    conn.execute(text("""
        CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS docs (
          id BIGSERIAL PRIMARY KEY,
          tenant_id TEXT NOT NULL,
          body TEXT,
          embedding vector(1536)
        )"""))
    conn.execute(text("""
        CREATE INDEX IF NOT EXISTS docs_emb_idx
        ON docs USING hnsw (embedding vector_cosine_ops)"""))

# Insert with vector (psycopg adapts np arrays)
with engine.begin() as conn:
    conn.execute(text("""
        INSERT INTO docs (tenant_id, body, embedding)
        VALUES (:t, :b, :e)"""),
        {"t": "acme", "b": text_, "e": vec})

# Semantic search + tenant filter in ONE query
with engine.connect() as conn:
    rows = conn.execute(text("""
        SELECT id, body FROM docs
        WHERE tenant_id = :t
        ORDER BY embedding <=> :q
        LIMIT 5"""),
        {"t": "acme", "q": query_vec}).all()

# Migrations: alembic revision --autogenerate -m "init"
annot: pool_pre_ping=True — stale connections self-heal at checkout
<=> is cosine distance; combine with WHERE freely — that's the pgvector edge
Alembic manages the schema from here on — never ALTER by hand in prod

notes:
# SQL from Python

## SQLAlchemy
- **Core**: SQL expression builder — composable, parameterized (Dapper-plus).
- **ORM**: declarative classes + session — the EF Core twin.
- `create_engine(url)` once, app-wide.

## SQL Server from Python
- `mssql+pyodbc://…` (ODBC Driver 18+); Trusted_Connection / Entra auth via ODBC.
- The ORM protects you from injection; raw SQL needs bound params — always.

## Pooling
- `pool_size=5, max_overflow=10, pool_pre_ping=True` — sane baseline.
- More replicas > bigger pools. Databases like many small polite clients.

## Alembic
- `alembic revision --autogenerate` → review → commit → `upgrade head` in CI/CD.
- Downgrade functions are your 3am rollback drill. EF Migrations, same religion.

## Postgres
- The AI-era default: free, ubiquitous, extension-rich. `postgresql+psycopg://…`.

## pgvector
- `vector(1536)` column + HNSW index → `ORDER BY embedding <=> $1 LIMIT k`.
- Vectors + relational filters + tenant isolation in ONE database — no sync, one backup.
- Limits vs dedicated stores: GA-10.
